procedure: Take a magnetic compass. Put it on a table and see which end of its needle points north. The N-pole of the needle is usually coloured red.
Place a bar magnet on the table. Bring the compass near to its N-pole. Observe the direction in which the N-pole of the needle stays.
Put the compass near to the S-pole of the bar magnet. Observe the direction in which the N-pole of the needle stays.
Place an iron nail with its head in contact with any pole of the bar magnet.

Put the compass near to the pointed end of the iron nail. Observe the direction in which the N-pole of the needle settles. Check whether the nail has become a magnet and magnetism has been induced in it.
Take the bar magnet away from the nail. Bring the compass near to the nail’s ends again and check whether the magnetism vanishes.
aim: To observe induced magnetism in an iron nail using a bar magnet and a magnetic compass.

viva.question: What is induced magnetism?
viva.answer: It is magnetism produced in a magnetic material by the influence of a nearby magnet.

viva.question: Which pole is induced at the end of the nail nearest to the magnet’s S-pole?
What pole is induced at the far end of the nail?
What happens to the nail’s magnetism when the bar magnet is removed?
How can you identify the N-pole of a compass needle?
viva.answer: It is the end that points north; it is usually coloured red.

diagram: Draw a bar magnet labelled N at its left end and S at its right end, with an iron nail touching the magnet’s S-pole; label the nail’s near end N and pointed far end S, and draw a compass beside the pointed end with its dial labelled N, E, S and W.
title: Induced magnetism in an iron nail
precautions: Keep the compass on a level table and away from other magnets or magnetic objects.
Identify the compass needle’s N-pole before bringing the bar magnet near it.
Bring the compass close to the nail’s pointed end without touching it.
Keep the nail in contact with the magnet while checking for induced magnetism, then remove the magnet to check whether the effect vanishes.
result: The bar magnet induces magnetism in the iron nail. The end near the magnet’s S-pole becomes an N-pole, while the far end becomes an S-pole; the induced magnetism vanishes when the magnet is removed.
